The 'survivor' is preferred only because we implicitly assume that what worked in the past (surviving tests) will work in the future, which is the very principle of uniformity Popper sought to eliminate.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If one can formulate a purely logical rule of preference that does not rely on future prediction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'acting on' a theory is distinct from 'believing' it will succeed, allowing for a non-inductive pragmatism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the rejection of rival theories provides sufficient negative justification without needing positive inductive support for the survivor.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Inductive Leakage Analysis: When Popper advises acting on the best-tested theory, he implicitly relies on the premise that 'past test performance predicts future utility.' Without this premise, the fact that Theory A survived 100 tests and Theory B failed 1 provides no rational basis for preferring A for a new application. The 'decision' to prefer A is thus cryptically inductive. The system survives only by pretending this practical necessity is a logical rule, but the underlying engine is Humean induction.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
